name: The Bread Tree of Pianello (l'Arbre a Pain)

location.address: Chataigneraie below the village of Pianello, Castagniccia, Haute-Corse, Corsica, France

access: Free, no ticket or gate reported. Stands in a communal chestnut grove (chataigneraie) below Pianello village in the Castagniccia forest, reached by a path rather than a road; local school groups and a TF1 news crew have visited it, which points to open access, but the exact route was not independently confirmed from these sources.
transport: Rural Corsica, no public transport. Nearest town is Piedicroce; a car and then a short walk down into the chestnut grove below Pianello village.
verify_notes: COORDINATE WARNING: the contest page's own GPS (N42 17'58.92'' E9 14'9.85'' = 42.2997, 9.236069, the coordinate given in the brief) is wrong by roughly 10km: it sits well west of Pianello. Wikipedia gives Pianello commune's own centre at 42.2906, 9.3608, which matches arbredelannee.com's tree coordinate (42.2903485, 9.3598147) almost exactly. Used the latter; still village/grove-level rather than a tree-level pin, hence approximate. Local name is 'l'Arbre a Pain' (the Bread Tree), so called because the chestnut was a staple food; also used historically to fatten pigs. Circumference of 15m and height of at least 12m is corroborated identically across three independent sources (arbredelannee.com, corsenetinfos, france3-regions), all citing the tree's 2014 French 'Arbre de l'Annee' award (jury prize) before it went on to the 2015 European contest (12th place, 654 votes). 15m circumference is exceptional even for chestnut, but the tree is described as having a thick base with numerous spherical burr-like protrusions (multi-stem/coppiced growth is typical of ancient sweet chestnuts), so the figure is plausibly a base/burr measurement rather than a clean single trunk; note this for the writer, do not state it as a smooth single-trunk girth without the caveat. Age 800-1000 years is the contest's own estimate, repeated identically by all secondary sources, no single documented planting date. The wider forest below Pianello (50 hectares of centuries-old chestnuts) has been studied by a European scientific research group for over a decade as of a 2023 article, which is good evidence of continued vitality and of the tree(s) being actively monitored, though it addresses the grove rather than this one named specimen by name. No source states current-year (2026) condition; nearest dated confirmation is the 2022/2023 research-group mentions of the surrounding grove.

name: Tamme-Lauri Oak

location.address: Tamme-Lauri, Urvaste kula, Antsla vald, Voru maakond, Estonia; signed off the Urvaste-Kanepi highway

access: Free, open year-round, no gate or ticket. Stands in a clearing beside a road, signposted from the Urvaste-Kanepi highway; a public tourist site, not private land.
transport: Rural southeastern Estonia, no public transport to the site itself. Nearest towns are Antsla and Urvaste; a car is the practical way to reach it, with the tree a short walk from roadside parking.
verify_notes: Estonia's largest and oldest tree by girth, and a genuinely famous single specimen: it was pictured on the reverse of the old 10 kroon banknote and is the reason this whole nomination clears the single-famous-tree bar. Girth 831cm measured at 130cm above ground (monumentaltrees.com and international Oak Society both give 8.0-8.5m depending on year/source; used the more precise 831cm figure). Height about 17m, reduced from taller by repeated lightning strikes over the centuries, which also hollowed the trunk; the hollow was filled with 8 tonnes of reinforced concrete in 1970 (structural repair, tree is otherwise healthy and still growing per multiple tourism sources). AGE BASIS IS UNUSUALLY STRONG for this project: a 1998 dendrochronological ring-count study dated planting to 1326, which makes it 700 years old in 2026, matching the contest's own 'about 700 years' almost exactly (visitestonia.com's rounder 'approximately 800 years' is the outlier and is the vaguer/older-sounding figure, so preferred the ring-study number). Name comes from local folklore: 'Tamme-Lauri' after Laurits/Lauri, a fire deity believed to inhabit the oak; a folk legend also claims a Swedish king's carriage axle got stuck in the ground on this spot and grew into the tree. The hollow trunk is said to fit seven people standing inside. Coordinates from the contest page convert cleanly to the brief's 57.917219, 26.576667 and match a named, signposted tourist site, so confirmed rather than approximate.

name: The Oak from Cajvana

location.address: Stejarul Secular din Cajvana, town of Cajvana, Suceava County, Romania (a plaque and bas-relief stand beside the tree)

access: Free, open, no gate. Stands in the town of Cajvana with a plaque and bas-relief beside it, and the town hall itself hosts a 24/7 public live webcam pointed at the tree, which is strong evidence it is a normal, openly visitable town monument rather than restricted land.
transport: Cajvana is a small town in Suceava County, northeastern Romania; nearest larger town/rail access is Suceava, roughly 25km away. No public transport directly to the tree; reachable by car or local bus into Cajvana, then on foot in town.
verify_notes: Declared a natural monument by the Romanian Academy in 1942, and reported (adevarul.ro, suceava.online) as the largest oak in southeastern Europe and among the top ranked in Europe by circumference. AGE BASIS IS STRONG: specialists carried out radiocarbon dating and concluded roughly 810 years, plus or minus 75 (so a range of about 735 to 885 years), independently supporting the contest's own 'approximately 750 years'; used the more specific radiocarbon figure and its stated error margin for age_min/age_max. Height 22.4m (one source) to 23m (another, the town hall's own page), circumference 11 to 11.01m (1101cm), consistent across three independent sources. Two legends attach to it, both flagged as legend rather than fact by the sources themselves: that it was planted around 1241 after the Tatar invasion, marking a mass grave; and that in 1476 Moldavian prince Stefan cel Mare rested his troops in its shade and was served traditional cas cheese there, supposedly the source of the town's name. The town hall's own live camera feed is itself a form of continued, dated evidence of the tree standing and being cared for as living heritage ('patrimoniu viu').

name: The Guardian of Cibin (Paznicul Cibinului)

location.address: Cheile Cibinului (Cibin Gorge), on the forest road toward Craciuneasa, about 12km from Gura Raului village, Marginimea Sibiului, Sibiu County, Romania

access: Free, no ticket. Stands beside a forest road/marked hiking trail with safety railings inside the Cheile Cibinului gorge, part of a signposted regional trail network (connecting toward Paltinis and Saua Canaia); managed by the Gura Raului forestry district (Ocolul Silvic Gura Raului). Genuinely open public forest land, not private.
transport: No public transport. Reached by car to Gura Raului village (Marginimea Sibiului, south of Sibiu city), then about 12km along a forest road into the Cibin gorge, on foot for the final stretch on the marked trail.
verify_notes: BRIEF'S OWN CAVEAT CONFIRMED AND RESOLVED: this tree is not near Sibiu city, it stands deep in the Cibin Gorge (Cheile Cibinului) above Gura Raului village in the Marginimea Sibiului region, roughly 12km up a forest road from the village. The contest's coordinate (45.73, 23.984167) is consistent with this area (well southwest of Sibiu, in the Cindrel/Cibin mountains) but no independent source gave its own GPS to cross-check the exact tree location against, hence approximate rather than confirmed, despite the site being a specific, named, marked trail landmark. Local Romanian name is 'Paznicul Cibinului' (the Guardian/Watchman of Cibin), which the contest translated as 'Guardian of Cibin'; note the contest's English name called it 'Multisecular Fir Tree, Guardian of Cibin'. SPECIES CHECK: Romanian news search results initially machine-translated 'brad' as 'spruce', which would have been wrong; 'brad' specifically means fir (Abies alba) in Romanian, distinct from 'molid' (spruce, Picea abies), and adevarul.ro's own headline and body confirm 'brad'/fir, matching the contest's Latin name. Height 42m (most sources; one headline rounds to 40m), trunk diameter about 2m at the widest point ('eight men can barely embrace it'), giving circumference/girth of roughly 628cm (2m diameter x pi), which is DERIVED from a diameter figure repeated by multiple sources rather than a directly stated circumference; flag this conversion for the writer. Age approximately 500 years is the contest's and every Romanian source's figure, traced in local lore to having emerged 'in the time of Mihai Viteazul' (Michael the Brave, reigned 1593-1601), which is consistent with roughly 500 years by 2026. CONFIRMED RECENTLY ALIVE: two independent 2024-09 articles (oradesibiu.ro, sibiuindependent.ro) describe it as currently standing and drawing tourists, so this is well within the 'alive in the last few years' bar. Legend: a shepherd sheltered sheep under the tree in a storm, they vanished, his tears/prayers made the tree miraculously grow tall enough that he climbed it and spotted his flock in a distant meadow; this legend is the origin of the name 'Guardian/Watchman'.

name: The Chestnut of Vales (Castanheiro de Vales)

location.address: Vales, near the Roman gold-mining site of Tresminas, Vila Pouca de Aguiar, Vila Real District, Portugal

access: ACCESS NOTE FOR THE WRITER/CURATOR: this tree stands on PRIVATE agricultural land, but multiple independent Portuguese sources (florestas.pt, and others via search) report that the owner has a standing, publicly reported invitation for anyone passing by to enter the land and view the tree ('o seu proprietario convida todos os que por la passam a entrar no terreno e contemplar o motivo do seu orgulho'). This is a genuine, sourced, standing invitation rather than a one-off, but it remains someone's working land rather than a park or churchyard; flag for a judgement call against hard rule 10 rather than treating it as unambiguously open like a public park.
transport: Rural Vila Real district, northern Portugal. No public transport to the site; nearest town is Vila Pouca de Aguiar, reached from Vila Real or Chaves by car; the tree stands near the Tresminas Roman gold-mine archaeological site.
verify_notes: Winner of Portugal's own 'Arvore do Ano' (Tree of the Year) 2020 before going on to place 6th in the European contest with over 17,000 votes. Classified by ICNF (Instituto da Conservacao da Natureza e das Florestas, Portugal's forestry/nature agency) as an 'Arvore de Interesse Publico' (Tree of Public Interest), which is an official register designation and counts as one of the two sources on its own per BRIEF_RESEARCH.md. Circumference 14m (1400cm) and height 21m repeated identically across florestas.pt, wilder.pt and the municipal Vila Pouca de Aguiar page; reported as the largest/thickest living chestnut tree in Portugal. The contest page's own figure ('4.5m trunk width') is very likely a rough diameter estimate rather than the circumference (14m circumference / pi = about 4.46m diameter, which matches almost exactly), so the two figures agree once you notice one is diameter and one is circumference; used the circumference for girth_cm and flagged this unit confusion so nobody double-counts it as a second, conflicting measurement. Age is given only vaguely and identically as 'about 1,000 years' or 'millennial' across every source, no documented planting date or ring study found, hence the wide age_min/age_max band rather than a tight figure. Local legend/history: believed associated with the Roman gold-mining operations at nearby Tresminas (one of the largest Roman gold mines in the Iberian peninsula), and remembered locally as the site of children's games across generations, with its hollow trunk cavity described as holding these stories. Coordinates convert cleanly from the contest's own GPS to the brief's 41.462417, -7.520492; no independent source gave a separate GPS to cross-check against, so marked approximate rather than confirmed.

name: The Three-Legged Oak (Encina de las Tres Patas)

location.address: La Laguna woodland, halfway between the village of Mendaza and the Santa Coloma hermitage, Mendaza, Navarra, Spain, at about 722m elevation

access: Free, no ticket or gate. Listed as a protected natural monument (see below); stands in woodland reached by a path between Mendaza village and the Santa Coloma hermitage. Government of Navarra's environment department has itself carried out conservation work on the tree (steel bolts in 1993), consistent with it being on accessible public/communal land rather than an enclosed private estate.
transport: Rural Navarra, no public transport to the site. Nearest towns are Estella-Lizarra and the villages of the Valle de la Berrueza; reachable by car to Mendaza, then on foot along the path toward the Santa Coloma hermitage.
verify_notes: COORDINATE ERROR IN THE BRIEF, CORRECTED: the contest's published GPS (N42 38'35.22'' W0 30'25.68'' = 42.643117, -0.507133, the coordinate given in the brief) is wrong by roughly 140km. Mendaza village's real location is confirmed by multiple independent sources (Wikipedia gives 42.64162, -2.234998; the Mendaza town hall's own page for this exact tree gives 42 38'34'' N, 2 13'36'' W = 42.6428, -2.22667) to be in western-central Navarra near Estella-Lizarra, not near the Ebro/Tudela area the contest's longitude (0 30' W) would place it. Used the town hall's own tree-specific coordinate (which states the tree stands at 722m elevation 'halfway between the town of Mendaza and the Santa Coloma hermitage', in a spot called 'La Laguna'), hence confirmed rather than approximate. Officially listed in the 'Catalogo de Arboles Monumentales de Navarra' since 1991 (a government register, which alone would be enough to deliver per BRIEF_RESEARCH.md, and here it is corroborated by press besides). In 1993 the Navarran government's environment department fitted two large steel bolts to stitch a crack near the base, and in 2000 neighbours added a metal band, both described as having saved the tree from collapse; this is good, dated evidence of continued, monitored vitality alongside general fragility. Measurements from mendaza.es and okdiario.com agree: circumference (perimetro) 7.70m at breast height, height 15.50m, and an unusually wide crown diameter of 19.20m for the trunk size. Age 'approximately 1,200 years' is repeated by every source and okdiario.com calls it Spain's second-longest-living tree and one of the oldest living things on the Iberian peninsula; no ring study or planting record given, hence the age_min/age_max band rather than a tighter figure. Its structure, an entirely hollow trunk standing only on three thick buttress-like sections ('legs'), is the source of the name and is itself the visual spectacle; local tradition holds that townspeople visit it regularly (the contest page mentions weekly visits) to pay respect.

name: The Seja Oak (Sejas ozols)

location.address: Edge of the former Seja Manor park, about 160m west of the Seja manor ruins, Seja, Saulkrasti Municipality, Latvia

access: Free, no ticket. Stands at the edge of a former manor park described as well maintained (mowed grass, raked paths), consistent with a managed public park rather than closed private land; a Latvian nature-monument designation on a tree normally goes with public visitability.
transport: Saulkrasti Municipality, Latvia, inland from the Baltic coast town of Saulkrasti. No direct public transport to the site; reachable by car via the village of Seja, then a short walk to the old manor park.
verify_notes: SECOND COORDINATE ERROR IN THIS BATCH, CORRECTED: the contest's published GPS (N56 46'58.28'' E21 59'20.09'' = 56.782856, 21.988914, the coordinate given in the brief) is wrong by roughly 165km, placing the pin in western Latvia (Kurzeme, near Saldus) rather than at Seja, which is inland from Saulkrasti in central/northern Latvia. senvietas.lv independently gives 57.19861, 24.58916 for the actual tree, describing it as standing in the former Seja Manor park on a hillside, and a second independent source (aprinkis.lv) adds it stands specifically 'on the edge of the manor park, 160m west of the Seja manor ruins', which pins it precisely; used that coordinate and marked confirmed. OFFICIAL PROTECTION: the tree holds Latvia's 'dabas piemineklis' (nature monument) status, a government register designation that on its own would be enough to deliver per BRIEF_RESEARCH.md; here it is corroborated by several independent Latvian sources besides. AGE BASIS IS UNUSUALLY STRONG: Guntis Enins, a Latvian naturalist who has surveyed the country's biggest trees for over 50 years, refined the age estimate by ring-counting a broken branch and calculating from that, arriving at roughly 500 years, which matches the contest figure exactly; local tradition additionally traces the tree/manor's story to 1567, when Johan Seyge acquired Seja manor, which is consistent with (though not proof of) a roughly 500-year-old tree. Circumference at 1.3m height is given as 9.05m by senvietas.lv (2017 measurement) and 9.15m by aprinkis.lv; used 910cm as a reasonable midpoint and flagged the small discrepancy. Height 22m. Described in the literature as the fourth-largest oak in the Baltic states (senvietas.lv) or the second-thickest (aprinkis.lv summary); sources disagree on the exact superlative rank, so treat 'one of the biggest oaks in the Baltics' as the safe claim rather than a specific rank. One source (senvietas.lv) explicitly debunks a romanticised modern claim (a plaque at the site suggesting ancient Latvian chieftains met there as a sacred site) as having 'no convincing evidence' and being a recent invention; flag this so the story does not repeat it as fact. Local tradition holds a genuine, ongoing summer-solstice (Jani) gathering at the tree with flower decorations and folk songs, per the contest page.
